claim: Across divergent thinking, poetry, music and visual art, default and executive control networks, which usually oppose each other, tend to cooperate during creative work.
quote: the default and executive control networks, which can show an antagonistic relation, tend to cooperate during creative cognition and artistic performance
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
n: review of fMRI studies across several domains
transfer: Do not run generation and control as strict opposites. One call proposes loosely, a second holds the goal, and each sees the other. Descriptive model, not an algorithm.

claim: The review reads default network activity as spontaneous generation of candidate ideas drawn from long-term memory, and the control network as constraining that stream to the task goal.
quote: Default network activity during creative cognition appears to reflect the spontaneous generation of candidate ideas
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
transfer: Generate step: loose, memory-driven proposals. Control step: a goal-keeping filter. A procedure can be written from this split, but the split is a model, not a measured algorithm.

claim: In professional poets, default and control clusters were negatively correlated while generating new poems, and the correlation rose during revision. Evaluation recruits control more than generation does.
quote: During idea generation, the default and control network clusters were negatively correlated. However, during idea revision, the correlation between the networks increased
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
n: one poet study, as reported in the review
transfer: Two modes: generation with constraints relaxed, then evaluation with the control step on. Do not mix them in one prompt.

claim: In art students, generation drew on widespread default regions, while evaluation added control regions and raised default-control coupling.
quote: idea generation was associated with widespread activity of default regions, whereas idea evaluation was associated with both default (e.g., MPFC and PCC) and control network activity
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
n: one visual-artist study, as reported in the review
transfer: Evaluation is its own step with its own context (goal, criteria), not just more generation.

claim: In divergent thinking the posterior cingulate coupled with the salience network early and with control regions later, read as a switching step before control.
quote: the PCC showed early coupling with the right anterior insula and later coupling with the right DLPFC
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
n: one fMRI study, reported inside the review
transfer: Order matters: a gating step first, then control. Descriptive. A rule such as free first, control later is a guess from this.

claim: The review says control-network involvement depends on how goal-directed the creative task is. With no clear goal or relaxed constraints, coupling is weaker.
quote: the extent of control network involvement depends on the extent to which creative thought is constrained to meet specific task goals
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
transfer: Match constraint strength to the task: open prompts get weak constraints, goal-bound tasks a strong goal-keeper. Fits our NoveltyBench versus ARC split. Hypothesis, not tested in models.

claim: The review leaves out insight on purpose and lists open questions: which evaluation subprocesses matter, and which default-network processes matter for creativity.
quote: Notably, we do not address research on creative insight
title: Creative Cognition and Brain Network Dynamics
transfer: none. Scope caveat: these network findings concern divergent thinking and art, not single-answer insight.

claim: A connectome model fit on 163 people doing divergent thinking predicted held-out creative ability (r 0.30 in leave-one-out); in two small outside samples r was 0.35 and 0.28 for the high-creative network.
quote: the high-creative network predicted the creativity scores of held-out participants
title: Robust prediction of individual creative ability from brain functional connectivity
n: n=163 discovery; outside samples n=39 and n=54
transfer: none directly. Creativity is a distributed trait spanning default, salience and executive systems, which supports several cooperating roles rather than one.

claim: In a 405-person resting-state outside sample the prediction was weak (r 0.13 for the high-creative network, 0.11 for the low one), so effects shrink outside the discovery sample.
quote: Chinese resting-state sample (n = 405)
title: Robust prediction of individual creative ability from brain functional connectivity
transfer: none. Effect-size warning: do not build a design on one connectivity result.

claim: In two studies, both associative ability (semantic distance of fluency answers) and executive ability (broad retrieval, fluid intelligence) uniquely predicted the quality of divergent-thinking answers.
quote: we found substantial effects of both associative and executive abilities
title: The roles of associative and executive processes in creative cognition
n: two studies; sample sizes not read
transfer: Concrete proxy: embedding distance between ideas and the prompt, or between ideas, as a diversity filter. Pair it with a quality check, since distance alone predicted only part of quality.

claim: The quality of ideas rises over time in a divergent-thinking session (serial-order effect), replicated in many studies; higher fluid intelligence flattens the rise.
quote: the tendency for the creative quality of ideas to increase over time
authors: Beaty, Silvia, Nusbaum, Jauk, Benedek (citing Beaty & Silvia 2012)
title: The roles of associative and executive processes in creative cognition
n: cited as replicated; count not given
transfer: Do not stop at the first batch. Keep generating and expect later items to be less obvious. Caution: serial order inside one thread differs from independent samples, which is what our diverge mode uses.

claim: Latent-variable study: divergent-thinking creativity was predicted by working-memory updating and inhibition but not by shifting.
quote: Creativity was predicted by updating and inhibition, but not shifting
title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control
transfer: Inhibiting the obvious answer matters. A step that lists the obvious ideas first and bars repeats is a direct analogue. The updating finding is descriptive.

claim: Insight solutions differed from non-insight solutions in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus: higher fMRI activity, and an EEG gamma burst about 0.3 s before the insight response.
quote: a burst of high-frequency gamma-band activity occurred about 0.3 seconds before participants indicated an insight solution
title: Neural activity when people solve verbal problems with insight
transfer: none. We have no analogue of a temporal-lobe burst. Descriptive, and small samples.

claim: Brain activity before a problem appeared predicted whether it would later be solved with insight: more medial frontal and temporal activity before insight, more occipital activity before non-insight.
quote: Neural activity during a preparatory period, before participants saw verbal problems, predicted whether they would later solve those problems with or without self-reported insight
authors: Kounios, Frymiare, Bowden, Fleck, Subramaniam, Parrish, Jung-Beeman
title: The prepared mind: neural activity prior to problem presentation predicts subsequent solution by sudden insight
n: EEG and fMRI experiments; sample sizes not read (paywall)
transfer: Weak mapping: an inward-focused, low-distraction prelude (restate the problem, drop the surface view) before an impasse problem. Hypothesis only. A search result also described a later Drexel thesis on anagrams that found no single general preparatory state (thesis, not opened).

claim: The 2014 review defines insight as a sudden nonobvious reinterpretation, and reports right-hemisphere coarse semantic coding, inward-focused attention before solution, and resting-state differences between insight-prone and analytic solvers.
quote: internally focused attention preceding and during problem solving
title: The cognitive neuroscience of insight
n: review; abstract known only through a search-result summary
transfer: Two solving styles, insight and analytic, with person-level bias. Route by style only after an impasse, as our plan does. Descriptive; no step is specified.

claim: Incubation meta-analysis: 117 studies, 3,606 participants. Mean unbiased effect about 0.41 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.54), median 0.26; 85 of 117 effects were positive.
quote: The unweighted mean of the unbiased effect size estimate was 0.41, with a standard deviation of 0.71
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: Small to medium effect. A pause-and-return step is worth it only where cheap. Use the median 0.26 for planning.

claim: Incubation helped creative (divergent) problems more than linguistic or visual insight problems, and longer preparation before the break gave larger effects.
quote: Individuals solving creative problems were more likely to benefit from an incubation period than individuals solving linguistic and visual problems.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: Incubation suits open tasks, consistent with our result that divergence helps open prompts. Work hard first, then set the problem aside and return: a staged call with a gap.

claim: A break filled with a demanding task gave a smaller incubation effect. For linguistic problems an undemanding task beat rest. For visual problems incubation worked only after a long preparation that reached impasse.
quote: low cognitive demand tasks yielded a stronger incubation effect than did rest during an incubation period when solving linguistic insight problems
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
n: 117 studies; 12 of 14 creative-problem studies used demanding break tasks, so that cell is thin
transfer: Rule: incubate only after a real impasse. For a model, the break could be a light unrelated generation call, then a fresh return. Untested in models; what counts as rest for a model is unclear.

claim: Mind-wandering experiment: only an undemanding task during a 12-minute break raised Unusual Uses originality, and only on problems seen before the break. New problems did not improve.
quote: engaging in an undemanding task during an incubation period led to substantial improvements in performance on previously encountered problems
authors: Baird, Smallwood, Mrazek, Kam, Franklin, Schooler
title: Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation
transfer: Re-attempt the same problem after a loosely occupied gap. The gain on repeated items only means a return step, not a general loosening step.

claim: In Baird 2012 the condition effect on repeated problems was moderate (effect size 0.10 as printed), fluency did not differ, so the gain was in originality, not volume. Mind-wandering reports differed modestly (effect size 0.05).
quote: Participants in the undemanding-task condition reported significantly greater mind wandering
title: Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation
transfer: Score originality apart from count. The incubation gain showed in originality only, so our judge should not reward fluency.

claim: The authors note the Remote Associates Task gives inconsistent incubation effects, unlike the Unusual Uses Task, which is consistent and robust.
quote: unlike convergent-thinking tasks (such as the Remote Associates Task), which have been more prone to empirical inconsistencies
title: Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation
transfer: Single-answer convergent tasks gain least from incubation. Do not add a break to puzzle routes.

claim: Baird et al. suggest incubation may work because default and executive systems both contribute during mind wandering, and note both are active before solution of insight problems.
quote: engaging in tasks conducive to mind wandering could contribute to incubation by creating a situation in which default and executive systems mutually contribute
title: Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation
transfer: none. Speculation by the authors, not a result.

claim: Meta-analysis of 20 fMRI studies of divergent thinking (596 participants) found four clusters: left inferior parietal, left inferior frontal and precentral, superior and medial frontal, and right cerebellum. The authors link them to the semantic control network.
quote: divergent thinking activity is significantly related to the semantic control network
title: A meta-analysis of functional magnetic resonance imaging studies of divergent thinking using activation likelihood estimation
transfer: Divergent thinking leans on controlled retrieval from semantic memory, not free association alone. Supports retrieval with control, not pure random sampling. Quote is from the fetch summary, not checked against the page text.

claim: Meta-analysis of 57 fMRI studies (27 divergent thinking, 30 insight) found no overlapping clusters. Divergent thinking leaned on a default-network parietal node, insight on frontal control, parietal, cingulate and hippocampus-amygdala regions.
quote: The conjunction analysis found no shared clusters between DT and insight
title: Uncovering neural distinctions and commodities between two creativity subsets: a meta-analysis of fMRI studies in divergent thinking and insight using activation likelihood estimation
transfer: Treat open divergence and single-answer insight as different procedures, as our route table does. The paper's System 1 versus System 2 reading is an interpretation. Quote is from the fetch summary, not checked against the page text.

claim: Novel metaphor production showed early default-salience coupling followed by later default-executive coupling, a second case of the same switch pattern as divergent thinking.
quote: early coupling of default (left AG) and salience (right anterior insula) regions that preceded later coupling of the left AG and left DLPFC
title: Brain networks underlying novel metaphor production
transfer: A staged order, loose then controlled, is a plausible schema step but has not been shown to improve output.
